question: In the 1820s, weavers at the Gobelins tapestry works complained that their black wool looked dull. What was wrong with the dye?
answer: Nothing. The chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul, hired to improve the dyes, found the blacks were sound: they looked weak because of the colours woven beside them. Each colour pushes its neighbour towards its opposite. His 1839 book on this contrast taught later painters, Seurat above all, to plan colours in pairs.
move: Before blaming the thing itself, look at what sits next to it.
ask: Is something in my life looking dull only because of what I have put beside it?
source: Chevreul, On Simultaneous Contrast of Colours, 1839
reference: Michel-Eugène Chevreul, The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colors (1839), ed. Faber Birren, Reinhold, 1967
